## a

Abolition 2000

Abolition 2000: Founded in 1995 during the NPT Review and Extension Conference, Abolition 2000 is an international non-governmental global network working for a treaty to eliminate nuclear weapons within a time-bound framework. The coalition consists of over 2,000 organizations from 90 different countries that work both independently and in concert to accomplish the goal of nuclear abolition through an eleven point program.

Acheson-Lilienthal Proposal

A U.S. initiative to outlaw nuclear weapons and to internationalize global stocks of fissile material for use in peaceful nuclear programs which became know as the Baruch Plan. See entry for [Baruch Plan](https://www.nti.org/education-center/glossary/#entry-baruch-plan).

Active Defenses

Active defenses use weapon systems or countermeasures to defend against an attack. See entry for [Passive Defenses](https://www.nti.org/education-center/glossary/#entry-passive-defenses)

Ad Hoc Group of Governmental Experts to Identify and Examine Potential Verification Measures from a Scientific and Technical Standpoint (VEREX)

VEREX: Created in September 1991 during the Third Review Conference of the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention (BTWC), VEREX was tasked with identifying measures that could be used to determine whether a state party to the BTWC is "developing, producing, stockpiling, acquiring, or retaining" biological weapons (BW). In its final report of September 24, 1993, VEREX described and analyzed 21 such measures, including but not limited to declarations of biological agents, on-site inspections, and multilateral information sharing.

Adamsite

Adamsite: A chemical agent that causes eye, nose, and respiratory tract irritation in addition to vomiting and diarrhea. Classified as a vomiting agent, adamsite is odorless and usually enters the body by inhalation. Upon entering the body, adamsite poisoning begins within minutes and lasts up to several hours. First synthesized in 1918, adamsite was used by the Japanese during World War II. While some have stockpiled adamsite as a riot-control agent, the OPCW Scientific Advisory Board recommends against such use.

Additional Protocol

The Additional Protocol is a legal document granting the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) complementary inspection authority to that provided in underlying safeguards agreements. The principal aim is to enable the IAEA inspectorate to provide assurance about both declared and possible undeclared activities. Under the Protocol, the IAEA is granted expanded rights of access to information and sites, as well as additional authority to use the most advanced technologies during the verification process. See entry for [Information Circular 540](https://www.nti.org/education-center/glossary/#entry-information-circular-540-).

Advanced Cruise Missile (ACM)

Advanced Cruise Missile (ACM): See entry for [Cruise missile](/glossary/cruise-missile).

Aegis

Aerosol

Aerosol: A system of liquid or solid particles uniformly distributed in a finely divided state through a gas, usually air. Because aerosols are a means for delivering chemical and biological agents, they can play an important role in weaponizing these substances.

African Nuclear-Weapon-Free-Zone

The Treaty on the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free-Zone, also known as the [Treaty of Pelindaba](https://www.nti.org/education-center/glossary/#entry-treaty-pelindaba), was opened for signature in Cairo in April 1996. The treaty prohibits the research, development, manufacturing, stockpiling, acquisition, testing, possession, control, and stationing of nuclear explosive devices on any member’s territory. The treaty also prohibits the dumping of radioactive waste originating from outside the continent within the region. In addition, the treaty requires parties to apply International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards to all their peaceful nuclear activities. The **Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): রূপপুর পারমাণবিক বিদ্যুৎ কেন্দ্র) is a 2.4 [GWe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GWe "GWe") nuclear power plant in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[5]](#cite_note-5) It consists of two 1200 MWe [VVER-1200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VVER "VVER") reactors. The nuclear power plant is located at Rooppur in [Ishwardi Upazila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishwardi_Upazila "Ishwardi Upazila") on the bank of the river [Padma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma "Padma"), about 160 km northwest of [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka").[[6]](#cite_note-6) It is the country's first [nuclear power plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_plant "Nuclear power plant"), and the first of the two units is expected to become operational in 2026.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Safety review by the [IAEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") was successfully completed in late 2025.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg/250px-Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg)

Satellite image of the power plant and surrounding area in January 2024

[Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") first conceived building a [nuclear power plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_plant "Nuclear power plant") in 1961. The [Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Atomic_Energy_Commission "Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission") was established in 1973. The country currently operates a [TRIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRIGA "TRIGA") research reactor at the Atomic Energy Research Establishment in [Savar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savar_Upazila "Savar Upazila").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Ruppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_2024.jpg/250px-Ruppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_2024.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ruppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_2024.jpg)

[Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant"), Rooppur, [Pabna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pabna_District "Pabna District")

More recently, in 2001 Bangladesh adopted a national Nuclear Power Action Plan.[[2]](#cite_note-nip102-2) On 24 June 2007, Bangladesh's government announced plans to build a nuclear power plant to meet electricity shortages.[[3]](#cite_note-energydaily1-3) In May 2010, Bangladesh entered into a civilian nuclear agreement with the [Russian Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Federation "Russian Federation"). It also has framework agreements for peaceful nuclear energy applications with the US, France and China.

In February 2011, Bangladesh reached an agreement with Russia to build the 2,400 [megawatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megawatt "Megawatt") (MW) [Ruppur Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Ruppur Nuclear Power Plant") with two reactors, each of which will generate 1,200 MW of power. The nuclear power plant will be built at Rooppur, on the banks of the [Padma River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_River "Padma River"), in the Ishwardi subdistrict of [Pabna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pabna_District "Pabna District"), in the northwest of the country.

The inter-governmental agreement (IGA) was officially signed on 2 November 2011.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
Estimated cost of the contract is US$12.65 billion.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) As per the Revised Annual Development Programme for 2024-2025, a total of BDT 73,746.06 crore had been spent on the project by June 2024.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

On 29 May 2013 Bangladesh's Prime Minister declared that a second 2 GW nuclear power plant will be constructed in the southern region of the country. In 2019, site selection was still in progress, with a focus on the coastal region at the Bay of Bengal.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Bangladesh received the first shipment of uranium fuel from Russia for its first nuclear power station in October 2023, making it the world's 33rd nuclear energy producer.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

On 28 April 2026, fuel loading began at unit-1 of the Rooppur plant, transitioning the project into the commissioning phase. The first 300 MW are expected to be added to the national grid by late July or early August 2026, with full 1,200 MW output from the first unit anticipated by early 2027.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

![Afif Hossain](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/story/media_bank/202310/afif-hossain-042240610-16x9.jpg?VersionId=5h1EQqaAEOjJ6miFqtOHAQpiWSMEpmgT&size=690:388 "All-round Afif Hossain helped Bangladesh beat Malaysia in the men's cricket quarter-final (AFP Photo)")

New Delhi,UPDATED: Oct 4, 2023 16:53 IST

Bangladesh came up with a sensational win over Malaysia in a last-over thriller in the quarter-final of men's cricket in the Asian Games 2023.Â

Afif Hosain successfully defended 5 runs in the final over of a thrilling cotest in which Malaysia gave a good account of themselves. Malaysia, chasing 117, were 112 for 7 with Virandeep Singh batting not out at 52. However, the star batter was not able to finish the game for Malsyaia and seal a place in the quarter-final as he was out to Afif Hossain in the 4th delivery of the final over for 52.

Afif gave only 2 singles in the last two bals to make sure Bangladesh held their nerves and sneaked into the semi-final of the men's cricket competition at the Asian Games.Â

Bangladesh will take on India in the semi-final on October 5.Â

**[Asian Games 2023: Updates](https://www.indiatoday.in/sports/asian-games-2023/story/asian-games-day-11-live-updates-neeraj-chopra-javelin-final-athletics-archery-boxing-men-hockey-team-2444054-2023-10-04)**

Bangladesh reached 116 for 5 in 20 overs as they struggled to get going at the top. Parvez Hossain and Mahmudul Hasan oy were dismissed for 0 as Bangladesh got off to the worst possible start. Zakir Hassan, Â who came in at No. 3, managed just 1.

However, captain Saif Hassan took the onus upon himself and scored a 50 helping Bangladesh recover from 3 for 3.Â

For Bangladesh, Afif and Ripon Mondol picked up 3 wickets each in a hard-fought bowling display to defend the sub-par total at Pingfeng Campus Cricket Field which has been host to some world-record scores.Â

Earlier on Tuesday, India defeated Nepal to in the men's cricket quarter-finals. The star of the match was undoubtedly Yashasvi Jaiswal, who delivered an exceptional performance with the bat. He scored a magnificent century, becoming the youngest Indian to score a T20I ton. His scintillating innings included eight fours and seven sixes, contributing to a total of 202 runs off just 49 balls. This impressive feat set the stage for India's victory, with the team finishing their innings at 202 runs for the loss of four wickets in the allotted 20 overs.

However, the match was not without its challenges for the Indian team. Despite the comfortable win, the bowlers faced some difficulties. Shivam Dube, despite being expensive, managed to bowl three overs, while Sundar, a front-line off-spinner, only bowled a solitary over. Arshdeep lacked his usual accuracy and sprayed the ball around. However, Bishnoi was superb, bagging three wickets and was ably supported by debutant Sai Kishore, who scalped a wicket and only gave away 24 runs in four overs.

Nepal put up a valiant fight, falling short by just 23 runs. They showed commendable spirit and resilience, providing a tough competition to the Indian team. Despite their loss, they demonstrated a template of how to play against the big teams.

The **Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): রূপপুর পারমাণবিক বিদ্যুৎ কেন্দ্র) is a 2.4 [GWe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GWe "GWe") nuclear power plant in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[5]](#cite_note-5) It consists of two 1200 MWe [VVER-1200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VVER "VVER") reactors. The nuclear power plant is located at Rooppur in [Ishwardi Upazila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishwardi_Upazila "Ishwardi Upazila") on the bank of the river [Padma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma "Padma"), about 160 km northwest of [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka").[[6]](#cite_note-6) It is the country's first [nuclear power plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_plant "Nuclear power plant"), and the first of the two units is expected to become operational in 2026.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Safety review by the [IAEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") was successfully completed in late 2025.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg/250px-Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rooppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant_Landsat-8_January_2024.jpg)

Satellite image of the power plant and surrounding area in January 2024

The plan to establish a nuclear power plant in the then [East Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Pakistan "East Pakistan") was made in 1961.[[9]](#cite_note-WNA-9) In 1963, the Rooppur village of the Pabna district was selected for the proposed plant and 260 acres of land was acquired.[[10]](#cite_note-profile-10)[[11]](#cite_note-:12-11) The plan was to establish a 200MW nuclear power plant on the selected site.[[11]](#cite_note-:12-11) The plan to construct a 200 MW power plant was completed in 1969 with the assistance of Belgium.[[12]](#cite_note-12) [Pakistan government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Pakistan "Government of Pakistan").[[13]](#cite_note-:10-13)

Bangladesh–Myanmar relations

|  |  |

[Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") and [Myanmar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar") have a complex relationship under the [military junta in Myanmar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_rule_in_Myanmar "Military rule in Myanmar"), and as a result of the presence of over 270,000 [Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohingya_refugees_in_Bangladesh "Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh"). The civil society and political class of Bangladesh have often expressed solidarity for Myanmar's pro-democracy struggle against military rule.

Relations between the two nations soured as a result of [Rohingya genocide](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohingya_genocide "Rohingya genocide") which resulted in the influx of over 1.1 million Rohingya refugees from [Rakhine State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakhine_State "Rakhine State") in Myanmar to Bangladesh.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Despite being neighbouring countries, very little trade exists among these countries.

Buddhism came to Myanmar in ancient times through Bengal. This shared Buddhist heritage was helpful in resisting the later British rule in the region, which expanded from Bengal outward to Myanmar (then Burma) in the 19th century.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The monk [U Ottama](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U_Ottama "U Ottama") played a significant role in promoting ties between Burma and [Bengali nationalists](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_nationalism "Bengali nationalism").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

## Contemporary Relations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bangladesh%E2%80%93Myanmar_relations&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Contemporary Relations")]

In May 1979, Burmese President [Ne Win](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Win "Ne Win") visited Bangladesh. During his visit, on 23 May, a demarcation agreement between the two countries was signed.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

[Operation Clean and Beautiful Nation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Clean_and_Beautiful_Nation "Operation Clean and Beautiful Nation") was a military operation conducted by the [Tatmadaw](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatmadaw "Tatmadaw") (Myanmar Armed Forces) in northern [Rakhine State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakhine_State "Rakhine State"), near Myanmar's border with Bangladesh in 1991. In December 1991, Tatmadaw soldiers crossed the border and accidentally fired on a Bangladeshi military outpost, resulting in [Bangladesh Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Army "Bangladesh Army") aiding [Rohingya Solidarity Organisation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohingya_Solidarity_Organisation "Rohingya Solidarity Organisation") as retaliation. The conflict ended in Burmese tactical failure.[[5]](#cite_note-Pulitzer-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Guardian1-7)

On 7 October 1998, between three and five Bangladeshi fishermen were killed by [Burmese Navy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burmese_Navy "Burmese Navy") forces just off the coast of [St. Martin's Island](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Martin's_Island "St. Martin's Island").[[8]](#cite_note-8) On 8 September 1999, one Bangladeshi fisherman was shot and killed by [Burmese Navy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burmese_Navy "Burmese Navy") forces near St. Martin's Island. Nine crewmen from the victim's fishing boat abandoned it, swam for their lives, and were rescued by Bangladeshi forces. The Bangladeshi government lodged a formal protest note to [Myanmar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar").[[9]](#cite_note-9) On 20 August 2000, the Bangladeshi police reported that Burmese border guards had shot and killed four Bangladeshi fishermen off the coast of St. Martin's Island.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The November [2008 Bangladesh–Myanmar naval standoff](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Bangladesh–Myanmar_naval_standoff "2008 Bangladesh–Myanmar naval standoff") caused the relations between two countries deteriorate, as Myanmar allowed the South Korean company [Daewoo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daewoo "Daewoo") to explore the seabed in an area southwest of [St. Martin's Island](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Martin's_Island "St. Martin's Island"), the area that was contested between Bangladesh and Myanmar as part of their respective exclusive economic zones.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Myanmar deployed two naval warships to protect its assets. The [bilateral relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilateral_relations "Bilateral relations") between the neighboring [People's Republic of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bangladesh "People's Republic of Bangladesh") and the [Republic of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_India "Republic of India") formally began in 1971 with India's recognition of an independent Bangladesh (which was formerly known as East Pakistan) following India's military intervention in support of the [Bangladeshi resistance forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukti_Bahini "Mukti Bahini") in their [war of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_liberation_war "Bangladesh liberation war") against [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan").

Although some disputes remain unresolved, the relations between the two countries have been characterised as cooperative.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Bangladesh and India are common members of [SAARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAARC "SAARC"), [BIMSTEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BIMSTEC "BIMSTEC"), [IORA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean_Rim_Association "Indian Ocean Rim Association") and the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations"). The two countries share many cultural ties. In particular, Bangladesh and the east Indian states of [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal") and [Tripura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripura "Tripura") are [Bengali-speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"). A historic land boundary agreement was signed on 6 June 2015 which settled decades-old [border disputes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India%E2%80%93Bangladesh_enclaves "India–Bangladesh enclaves"),[[4]](#cite_note-4) while negotiations are still ongoing over the sharing of water of the [transboundary rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transboundary_river "Transboundary river").

In recent years, Bangladesh has seen rising [anti-India sentiments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-India_sentiment "Anti-India sentiment") among its citizens due to the Indian government's perceived anti-Muslim and anti-Bangladeshi activities including India's interference in internal politics of Bangladesh, [killings of Bangladeshis by Indian BSF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaths_along_the_Bangladesh%E2%80%93India_border "Deaths along the Bangladesh–India border"), [Citizenship Amendment Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_Amendment_Act "Citizenship Amendment Act"), rise of [Hindutva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindutva "Hindutva") in India, [anti-Bangladeshi misinformation in Indian media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Bangladesh_anti-Hindu_violence#Misinformation "2024 Bangladesh anti-Hindu violence") as well as India's reluctance in solving the water disputes in common rivers with Bangladesh.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) In 2019, several Bangladeshi ministers cancelled their scheduled state visits to India as a response to India's Citizenship Amendment Bill.[[9]](#cite_note-ie13Dec2016-9) In 2021, [massive protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Bangladesh_anti-Modi_protests "2021 Bangladesh anti-Modi protests") in Bangladesh against the state visit by Indian PM Narendra Modi to the country led to the deaths of at least 14 people.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Furthermor

**2023** ([MMXXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numerals "Roman numerals")) was a [common year starting on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_year_starting_on_Sunday "Common year starting on Sunday") of the [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar "Gregorian calendar"), the 2023rd year of the [Common Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era") (CE) and *[Anno Domini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anno_Domini "Anno Domini")* (AD) designations, the 23rd year of the [3rd millennium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_millennium "3rd millennium") and the [21st century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_century "21st century"), and the 4th year of the [2020s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020s "2020s") decade.

 

It will follow 1429 and 1430 [Baṅgābda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_Era "Bengali Era") (Bengali Year).

The year 2023 is the 52nd year of the [independence of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_of_Bangladesh "Independence of Bangladesh"). It is also the fifth and last year of the [fourth cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Hasina_ministry "Fourth Hasina ministry") of Prime Minister [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") and last year of the presidency of [Mohammad Abdul Hamid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Abdul_Hamid "Mohammad Abdul Hamid").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Deaths along the Bangladesh–India border** occur many times a year as a result of people allegedly attempting to illegally cross or walk along the border, cross-border firing and suspected cattle smuggling.[[1]](#cite_note-hrw1-1) [Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") and [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") share a 4,096 km (2,545 mi) border.[[2]](#cite_note-2) To prevent suspected smuggling and illegal migration from Bangladesh, the Indian [Border Security Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF) exercises its controversial "shoot on sight" policy. Under this policy, the BSF can shoot any person on sight with or without cause.[[3]](#cite_note-guard1-3)

According to a report published by human rights organisations, around 1,000 Bangladeshi civilians were killed by the Indian BSF in a period of 10 years (from 2001 to 2010).[[4]](#cite_note-HR-4)[[5]](#cite_note-TheHindu-5) The report also states that Indian paramilitary forces routinely threaten, abuse, [arbitrarily detain](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_arrest_and_detention "Arbitrary arrest and detention"), and torture local Bangladeshi civilians living along the border, and Bangladeshi border guards usually do not help the Bangladeshi civilians.[[4]](#cite_note-HR-4)[[5]](#cite_note-TheHindu-5)[[6]](#cite_note-BBC-6)

### Bangladesh claims against Border Security Force

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deaths_along_the_Bangladesh%E2%80%93India_border&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Bangladesh claims against Border Security Force")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Indo_Bangladesh_Border%2C_Dakshin_Denajpur.jpg/250px-Indo_Bangladesh_Border%2C_Dakshin_Denajpur.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indo_Bangladesh_Border,_Dakshin_Denajpur.jpg)

In some border areas, strong fences are installed by India

The Indian [Border Security Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF) exercises its controversial "shoot on sight" policy to stop illegal migration. The then-head of BSF, Raman Srivastava, stated that people should not feel sorry for the victims as they were trying to illegally enter into India, and therefore they are a legitimate target.[[3]](#cite_note-guard1-3) Killings along the [Bangladesh–India border](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh–India_border "Bangladesh–India border") are routine and arbitrary. Around 1,000 people, mostly Bangladeshi nationals, were killed by Indian border security forces over the period of 10 years (2001 to 2010).[[4]](#cite_note-HR-4) None of the Indian BSF personnel involved in killings along the border were ever prosecuted.[[3]](#cite_note-guard1-3) A 2010 [Human Rights Watch](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") (HRW) report stated that BSF justified killing by claiming that it was an act of self-defence, or that the suspects were evading arrest.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:4-8) However, the reports filed by the BSF with the Indian police don't show recovery of any lethal weapon or explosives from the victim which justifies self-defense.[[8]](#cite_note-:4-8) Several survivors and eyewitnesses of BSF attacks allege that the BSF resorts to indiscriminate shooting without issuing any warning.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Human Rights Watch reports that the BSF, which has a long record of severe human rights abuses, is exempt from criminal prosecution, unless it is specifically ordered by the Indian government to undertake a prosecution in a particular case.[[8]](#cite_note-:4-8) [Brad Adams](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Adams "Brad Adams"), then the Asia director of Human Rights Watch, stated in 2011 that "Routinely shooting poor, unarmed villagers is not how the world's largest democracy should behave."[[3]](#cite_note-guard1-3)

While speaking about border killings in a 2022 interview, India-based human rights activist Kiriti Roy from Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha (MASUM) noted the existence of barbed wire fences in Indian territories that are within 150 yards from zero point ("no man's land"). He pointed out that per the Geneva Convention, defence infrastructure cannot be built within this 150-yard zone.[[9]](#cite_note-:5-9) In January 2025, BSF reportedly attempted to construct more barbed wire fences along the zero line in violation of the international law.

The **Bangladesh–India border**, known locally as the **Radcliffe line**, is an [international border](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_boundary "International boundary") running between the republics of [Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") and [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). Six [Bangladeshi divisions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisions_of_Bangladesh "Divisions of Bangladesh") and five [Indian states](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_and_union_territories_of_India "States and union territories of India") lie along the border.

Bangladesh and India share a 4,096-kilometre-long (2,545 mi) international border, the sixth-longest land border in the world,[[note 1]](#cite_note-1) including 262 km (163 mi) in [Assam](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam "Assam"), 856 km (532 mi) in [Tripura](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripura "Tripura"), 318 km (198 mi) in [Mizoram](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizoram "Mizoram"), 443 km (275 mi) in [Meghalaya](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meghalaya "Meghalaya") and 2,217 km (1,378 mi) in [West Bengal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal").[[1]](#cite_note-2) The Bangladeshi divisions of [Mymensingh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mymensingh_Division "Mymensingh Division"), [Khulna](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khulna_Division "Khulna Division"), [Rajshahi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajshahi_Division "Rajshahi Division"), [Rangpur](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangpur_Division "Rangpur Division"), [Sylhet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet_Division "Sylhet Division"), and [Chittagong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division") are situated along the border. A number of pillars mark the border between the two states. Small demarcated portions of the border are fenced on both sides.

[![Bangladesh](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Bangladesh_India_internal_border%2C_showing_Bangladesh_side.jpg/250px-Bangladesh_India_internal_border%2C_showing_Bangladesh_side.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bangladesh_India_internal_border,_showing_Bangladesh_side.jpg)

[![India](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Bangladesh_India_internal_border%2C_showing_India_side.jpg/250px-Bangladesh_India_internal_border%2C_showing_India_side.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bangladesh_India_internal_border,_showing_India_side.jpg)

The [Radcliffe Line](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_Line "Radcliffe Line") was published on 17 August 1947 as a boundary [demarcation line](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demarcation_line "Demarcation line") between the dominions of [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_India "Dominion of India") and [Pakistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan "Dominion of Pakistan") upon the [partition of India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India"). It was named after its architect, [Sir Cyril Radcliffe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Radcliffe,_1st_Viscount_Radcliffe "Cyril Radcliffe, 1st Viscount Radcliffe"), who, as chairman of the Border Commissions, was charged with equitably dividing 450,000 square kilometres (175,000 sq mi) of territory with 88 million people based on religious lines.[[2]](#cite_note-3) This involved the [partition of the Bengal region](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_Bengal_(1947) "Partition of Bengal (1947)"), which resulted in transferring [East Bengal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bengal "East Bengal") to Pakistan,[[3]](#cite_note-4) which was later [liberated in 1971](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War "Bangladesh Liberation War"), thereby Bangladesh continuing to share the same line as the border with the Indian Republic.

The **Karnaphuli Tunnel** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): কর্ণফুলী টানেল) is an underwater expressway tunnel in the port city of [Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong "Chittagong"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") under the [Karnaphuli River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnaphuli_River "Karnaphuli River"). The length of the entire route is 9.39 kilometres (5.83 mi), with the tunnel making up 3.32 kilometres (2.06 mi) of the length. The tunnel diameter is 10.80 metres (35.4 ft). It is expected, over 17,000 vehicles will be able to use this tunnel daily.[[1]](#cite_note-Dhaka-2023-2-1) The cost of the project is estimated at US$1.1B, of which around half is financed by the [Exim Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exim_Bank_of_China "Exim Bank of China").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-FinExpress-3) The Karnaphuli Tunnel is the first underwater road tunnel in South Asia.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[3]](#cite_note-FinExpress-3) It is expected to improve the [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka")–[Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong "Chittagong")–[Cox's Bazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox's_Bazar "Cox's Bazar") highway network.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) A Chinese company, [China Communications Construction Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Communications_Construction_Company "China Communications Construction Company"), was selected to construct it.[[9]](#cite_note-Dhaka-2019-9) The tunnel segments were produced in [Zhenjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhenjiang "Zhenjiang"), China.[[3]](#cite_note-FinExpress-3)

On 14 October 2016, the Bangladesh Prime Minister and Chinese President Xi Jinping laid the foundation stone of the project.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Prime Minister [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") and [Chinese Communist Party general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") inaugurated the construction site of the tunnel on 14 October 2017. [Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") officially inaugurated the construction of the tunnel and inaugurated the tunnel boring phase on 24 February 2019.[[3]](#cite_note-FinExpress-3)[[11]](#cite_note-Dhaka-2023-11) On 28 October 2023, Sheikh Hasina inaugurated the tunnel as **Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Tunnel** and was made available for traffic from 6 am the next day.[[1]](#cite_note-Dhaka-2023-2-1)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

It was renamed to **Karnaphuli Tunnel** on 26 February 2025 by the [Interim government of Bangladesh.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interim_government_of_Muhammad_Yunus "Interim government of Muhammad Yunus")[[13]](#cite_note-13)

The construction of the tunnel cost ৳10374 [crore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crore "Crore") (equivalent to ৳110 billion or US$930 million in 2024).[[11]](#cite_note-Dhaka-2023-11) In October 2016, during the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to Dhaka, the loan agreement for th

**United Nations peacekeeping** is the deployment of international military, police, and civilian personnel under [United Nations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") command to help countries transition from conflict to peace.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Authorized by the [United Nations Security Council](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") and administered by the [Department of Peace Operations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Peace_Operations "United Nations Department of Peace Operations"), it is one of the principal instruments through which the United Nations addresses threats to international peace and security. It is distinguished from [peacemaking](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaking "Peacemaking"), [peace enforcement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_enforcement "Peace enforcement"), and [peacebuilding](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacebuilding "Peacebuilding"), although these activities may overlap in practice.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)

Peacekeeping is not mentioned in the [United Nations Charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations "Charter of the United Nations"); it developed during the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") as an improvised response to crises the Security Council was unable to address through the originally planned [collective security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_security "Collective security") provisions. Peacekeeping is governed by three principles: there must be consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defense and defense of the mandate.[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4) The mandates of UN peacekeeping missions have expanded significantly over time, from early observer deployments to multidimensional operations which may support complex [peace agreements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_treaty "Peace treaty") or protect civilians in active conflicts under [Chapter VII of the UN Charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_VII_of_the_United_Nations_Charter "Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter"). Peacekeepers may include soldiers, police, and civilian participants; they wear their home countries' uniforms and **Blue Helmets** or **Blue Berets**, which have become synonymous with UN peacekeeping.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Since 1948, more than two million people from 125 countries have served in 72 UN peacekeeping operations; the forces were collectively awarded the [Nobel Peace Prize](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") in 1988.[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) As of 2026, eleven operations are active, with a combined budget of $5.66 billion and around 53,000 personnel deployed from 117 countries, the largest contributors being [Nepal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), [Rwanda](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda"), [Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"), [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), and [Pakistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"). Scholars have found that peacekeeping is associated with reduced conflict recurrence and fewer civilian casualties, although effectiveness varies with the local situation and a mission's mandate.

**Bangladesh–China relations**, also known as **Dragon–Tiger diplomacy**, refers to the bilateral relations between the [People's Republic of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bangladesh "People's Republic of Bangladesh") and the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China"). Both countries established formal diplomatic relations in January 1976. China has an embassy in [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka") and Bangladesh has one in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing") and consulates in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") and [Kunming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunming "Kunming"). Both countries are members of the [BCIM Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BCIM_Forum "BCIM Forum") (Bangladesh-China-India-Myanmar Forum for Regional Cooperation). According to Chinese government designations, Bangladesh and China are in a "comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership".[[1]](#cite_note-1)

### Bengal and Imperial China

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bangladesh%E2%80%93China_relations&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Bengal and Imperial China")]

Chinese monks, scholars and traders began frequenting [Bengal (Tosali Province)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantriparishad "Mantriparishad") from the [Qin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty") period. Famous ancient Chinese travelers to Bengal included [Faxian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faxian "Faxian"), [Yijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yijing_(monk) "Yijing (monk)") and [Xuanzang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuanzang "Xuanzang").[[2]](#cite_note-fmprc.gov.cn-2) During the [Pala Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pala_Empire "Pala Empire") of Bengal, [Atisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atisa "Atisa") of [Bikrampur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bikrampur "Bikrampur") traveled to [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet") and played an important role in developing Tibetan Buddhism.[[2]](#cite_note-fmprc.gov.cn-2)

In 648, a companion of [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), [Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa'd_ibn_Abi_Waqqas "Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas"), who is credited have introduced [Islam in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China "Islam in China"), is said to have followed a route via the [Brahmaputra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmaputra "Brahmaputra"). Evidence remains in [Lalmonirhat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalmonirhat_District "Lalmonirhat District") of a [masjid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid "Masjid") built by himself and is known locally as Abi Waqqas Masjid.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Political relations became nonexistent until the Middle Ages after the decline of Buddhism in South Asia.[[5]](#cite_note-5) After the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") conquest of Bengal in the 13th century, general [Bakhtiar Khilji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakhtiar_Khilji "Bakhtiar Khilji") attempted to invade Tibet.[[6]](#cite_note-Ahmed2011-6) Khilji's army was compelled to retreat due to the harsh conditions of the [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya"). [Ming China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_China "Ming China") and the [Bengal Sultanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate "Bengal Sultanate") exchanged many embassies during the 15th century. ### East Pakistan (or Modern day Bangladesh)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bangladesh%E2%80%93China_relations&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: East Pakistan (or Modern day Bangladesh)")]

Chinese premier [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai") visited [East Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Pakistan "East Pakistan") several times in the 1950s and 60s. The [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") maintained close ties with Bengali nationalist leaders [Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maulana_Abdul_Hamid_Khan_Bhashani "Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani") and [Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huseyn_Shaheed_Suhrawardy "Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy"). Sheikh Mujib in particular, was considered close to [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"). While serving as the Prime Minister of Pakistan in 1957, Awami League president H. S. Suhrawardy became the first Pakistani leader to make a state visit to the PRC.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Geopolitical relations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bangladesh%E2%80%93China_relations&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geopolitical relations")]

When the [Bangladesh War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_War_of_Independence "Bangladesh War of Independence") broke out in 1971, complex geopolitical rivalries erupted in South Asia. The Bangladeshis elicited the help of India in their freedom struggle. China had earlier fought a war with India in 1962 and became an ally of Pakistan. Crucially, it was using Pakistan as a conduit for [rapprochement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapprochement "Rapprochement") with [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") and [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger") in the United States. [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Kutupalong_Refugee_Camp_%28John_Owens-VOA%29.jpg/250px-Kutupalong_Refugee_Camp_%28John_Owens-VOA%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kutupalong_Refugee_Camp_(John_Owens-VOA).jpg)

[Kutupalong Refugee Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutupalong_Refugee_Camp "Kutupalong Refugee Camp") in [Cox's Bazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox's_Bazar "Cox's Bazar"), Bangladesh.

**Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh** are forcibly displaced [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar") nationals from [Rakhine State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakhine_State "Rakhine State") who are living in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) The [Rohingya people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohingya_people "Rohingya people") have experienced ethnic and [religious persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Muslims_in_Myanmar "Persecution of Muslims in Myanmar") in Myanmar for decades. Hundreds of thousands have fled to other countries in [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), including [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), and [the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines").[[3]](#cite_note-:14-3) The majority have [sought refuge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") in Bangladesh. In Bangladesh, two officially registered [refugee camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_camp "Refugee camp") are located in the sub-districts of Ukhiya and Teknaf in [Cox's Bazar District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox's_Bazar_District "Cox's Bazar District").[[4]](#cite_note-Milton2017-4) Violence in Myanmar has escalated in recent years, so the number of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh has increased rapidly. According to the [UN Refugee Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Refugee_Agency "UN Refugee Agency") (UNHCR), more than 723,000 Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since 25 August 2017.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-Minar2020-8)

A varicella outbreak was recorded in the refugee camp in December 2018, which spread rapidly among the inhabitants of the camp resulting in a total of 82,297 cases.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

On 28 September 2018, at the 73rd [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") (UNGA), Bangladeshi Prime Minister [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") said there were 1.1 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh by that time.[[3]](#cite_note-:14-3) Overcrowding from the recent population boom at Bangladesh's Rohingya refugee camps has placed a strain on their infrastructure. The refugees lack access to services, education, food, clean water, and proper sanitation; they are also vulnerable to [natural disasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_disaster "Natural disaster") and [infectious disease transmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathogen_transmission "Pathogen transmission").[[10]](#cite_note-Mahmood2017-10)[[11]](#cite_note-Chan2018-11)[[12]](#cite_note-:15-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Summers2018-13) As of June 2018, [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") announced nearly half a billion dollars in monetary support to help Bangladesh address Rohingya refugees' needs in areas including health, education, water and sanitation, disaster risk management, and social protection.[[14]](#cite_note-14) An August 2018 study estimated that more than 24,000 Rohingya had been killed by the [Myanmar military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatmadaw "Tatmadaw") and local [Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") militia since the "clearance operations" started on 25 August 2017. It also estimated that at least 18,000 Rohingya Muslim women and girls were raped, 116,000 Rohingya were beaten, and 36,000 Rohingya were thrown into fires set alight in an act of deliberate arson.[[15]](#cite_note-oida-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)

Rohingyas are a [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") minority in Myanmar regarded by many [Myanmar Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_Myanmar "Buddhism in Myanmar") as illegal migrants from Bangladesh, a controversial claim without strong evidence.[[8]](#cite_note-Minar2020-8)[[20]](#cite_note-20) The Rohingyas have lived in Myanmar for generations and the Bangladesh government has called on Myanmar to take them back.[[21]](#cite_note-21) They are denied citizenship in Myanmar and have been described as the world's most persecuted minority.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) Myanmar has denied persecuting the Rohingyas.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

The history of the Rohingya people can be broadly categorized into three distinct periods: precolonial, colonial, and postcolonial. In the precolonial era, the independent kingdom of Arakan (now Rakhine State) hosted diverse populations, including Muslim Arab sailors who arrived between 788 and 810 CE, and Bengali settlers who arrived between the 15th and 17th centuries.[[25]](#cite_note-Ahmed2014-25) During this period, Rohingyas and Arakanese Buddhists coexisted peacefully, sharing cultural and economic exchanges. However, this harmony was disrupted following British colonization in 1825, after the First Anglo-Burmese War. The division between these communities deepened further during World War II, when the Rohingyas allied with the British, while the Arakanese Buddhists sided with the Japanese.[[26]](#cite_note-26) This allegiance shift had dire consequences for the Rohingya, who became targets of mass violence during the Japanese occupation of Burma, with an estimated 100,000 killed and 50,000 forced into exile in East Bengal.[[25]](#cite_note-Ahmed2014-25)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Following Burma's independence in 1948, discrimination against the Rohingya intensified, with their rights and citizenship increasingly restricted. Between 1940 and 1947, Buddhist nationalist extremism gained momentum, further marginalizing the Rohingya population. The situation escalated in 1978, when the Burmese military junta launched a large-scale operation to expel those deemed "illegal inhabitants," resulting in widespread harassment, violence, and arbitrary arrests.[[4]](#cite_note-Milton2017-4) This led to the mass exodus of approximately 250,000 Rohingyas to Bangladesh. In response to international pressure, a repatriation agreement was reached between Burma and Bangladesh the following year, forcing most Rohingyas to return to Burma. However, just three years later, the 1982 Citizenship Law was enacted, formally revoking Rohingya citizenship and rendering an estimated 800,000 people stateless in northern Rakhine State. Despite undeniable historical evidence of Rohingya presence in Burma for centuries, the Burmese government has continued to deny their identity, refusing to recognize them as an official ethnic group. Instead, they are labeled "Bengali" illegal immigrants, perpetuating their exclusion, statelessness, and vulnerability to ongoing persecution.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Since the 1970s, Rohingya refugees have been coming to Bangladesh from Myanmar. In **Bangladesh's 2023 dengue epidemic season**, the country had witnessed the deadliest outbreak of [dengue fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dengue_fever "Dengue fever") ever since the first outbreak in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_in_Bangladesh "2000 in Bangladesh").[[1]](#cite_note-3)[[2]](#cite_note-4)[[3]](#cite_note-5) As of 31 December 2023, the [Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate_General_of_Health_Services_(Bangladesh) "Directorate General of Health Services (Bangladesh)") has reported 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths due to the *[Aedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aedes "Aedes")* [mosquito-borne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito-borne_disease "Mosquito-borne disease") [tropical disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_disease "Tropical disease") in the 2023 outbreak year.[[4]](#cite_note-6) Like previous years, the outbreak started in [Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer "Summer") (April–May), spread and surged nationwide in the [monsoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoons "Monsoons") (July–August).[[5]](#cite_note-:0-7) On 3 August, the number of deaths surpassed previous years; and on 21 August, the tally of hospitalization surpassed the previous highest record of the [2019 outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_dengue_outbreak_in_Bangladesh "2019 dengue outbreak in Bangladesh").[[6]](#cite_note-8) [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka") is the worst-hit area and the epicentre of the outbreak, with more than half of the cases being reported in the [megacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megacity "Megacity").[[7]](#cite_note-9)[[5]](#cite_note-:0-7) On 25 July, hospitalizations were reported in all districts; and the tally of hospitalizations outside Dhaka city surpassed the figure of the capital on 14 August.

In June 2023, the [Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Epidemiology,_Disease_Control_and_Research "Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research") reported that people are getting affected with the DENV-2 and DENV-3 variants this season, the two with the highest rates of infections and death.[[8]](#cite_note-10) In 2022 and 2021, DENV-4 and DENV-3 were found for the first time, respectively.[[9]](#cite_note-11)[[10]](#cite_note-12) Although a patient does develop immunity to a certain variant after being infected with it, cross-infection with different variants raises the chance of complications and mortality. Secondary infections show changed symptoms, thus delayed hospitalizations are causing more deaths. It's notable that the death rate has more or less increased in Bangladesh in past years.[[11]](#cite_note-13) With more severe cases being referred to the capital, Dhaka's hospitals struggle to control the situation.

General elections were held in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") on 7 January 2024 in accordance with the [constitutional requirement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bangladesh "Constitution of Bangladesh"), stating that elections must take place within the 90-day period before the expiration of the current term of the [Jatiya Sangsad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatiya_Sangsad "Jatiya Sangsad") on 29 January 2024. The [Awami League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League"), led by incumbent [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina"), won the election for the fourth consecutive time with less than 40% of the eligible voters voting according to an Election Commission, which was run by the ruling political party.[[4]](#cite_note-:3-5)[[5]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[6]](#cite_note-7)[[7]](#cite_note-:BBC-8) The party won 224 seats while independent candidates, most of whom were Awami League members propped up as [dummy candidates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_candidate "Dummy candidate") to give a semblance of competition, won 62 seats.[[8]](#cite_note-9)[[9]](#cite_note-:4-10)[[10]](#cite_note-11)

In the lead-up to the election, the incumbent government led by [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") cracked down on opposition parties and silenced critics of the government.[[11]](#cite_note-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13)[[13]](#cite_note-:2-14) Hasina's prime ministership has been described as authoritarian since being re-elected in 2008,[[14]](#cite_note-15)[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17)[[17]](#cite_note-18) and in 2011 removed the requirement that a temporary independent [caretaker government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caretaker_government "Caretaker government") be formed to hold elections. The main opposition party, the [Bangladesh Nationalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Nationalist_Party "Bangladesh Nationalist Party"), boycotted the elections (as they did in 2014) as they assumed that the election commission under the incumbent government were unable to organise a free and fair election.[[13]](#cite_note-:2-14)

A protest over the election turnout emerged as the Chief Election Commissioner initially claimed, based on the data at hand, that turnout was 28%, but later retracted that statement to claim turnout was around 40%.[[9]](#cite_note-:4-10)[[7]](#cite_note-:BBC-8)

Alamgir"), [Anisur Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anisur_Rahman_(economist) "Anisur Rahman (economist)"), [Rashida Sultana Emily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashida_Sultana_Emily "Rashida Sultana Emily") and [Ahsan Habib Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahsan_Habib_Khan "Ahsan Habib Khan").[[36]](#cite_note-37)

In the election, President [Mohammed Shahabuddin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shahabuddin "Mohammed Shahabuddin") and first lady [Rebecca Sultana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Sultana "Rebecca Sultana") used a postal ballot to cast their vote on 3 January 2024. It is the first instances of using postal ballot in the history of elections in Bangladesh.[[37]](#cite_note-38)

The 350 members of the Jatiya Sangsad consist of 300 directly elected seats using [first-past-the-post voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting "First-past-the-post voting") in single-member constituencies, and an additional 50 seats reserved for women. The reserved seats are selected by the elected constituency members via the [single transferable vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_transferable_vote "Single transferable vote"). Each parliament sits for a five-year term.[[38]](#cite_note-39)

The electoral system has been criticised as disproportional[[39]](#cite_note-40)[[40]](#cite_note-41)[[41]](#cite_note-:5-42) and a key driver of political deadlock in the country.[[41]](#cite_note-:5-42)

## Pre-electoral statistics and information

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2024_Bangladeshi_general_election&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pre-electoral statistics and information")]

According to the data released by the [Election Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Election_Commission "Bangladesh Election Commission") on 4 January 2024, the total number of voters in the next parliamentary election is 119,689,289 people. Among them, 60,769,741 are men voters, 58,918,699 are women voters and 849 hijra voters.[[42]](#cite_note-43) According to EC, 28 political parties and a total of 1,970 candidates are contesting the election, of which 436 are independent candidates. Total final polling centres are 42,148 and final polling booths are 261,564.[[43]](#cite_note-44)[[44]](#cite_note-45)

The BNP has demanded that there should be a caretaker government during election season because, as Citizens for Good Governance founder-secretary [Badiul Alam Majumder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badiul_Alam_Majumdar "Badiul Alam Majumdar") has claimed, every [election in Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Bangladesh "Elections in Bangladesh") that was not conducted under a caretaker government has been marred by irregularities.[[45]](#cite_note-46)[[27]](#cite_note-aa17Jan2023-28) Without a caretaker government, the BNP has stated its intent to boycott the elections. On 17 May 2023, BNP standing committee member [Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amir_Khasru_Mahmud_Chowdhury "Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury") said: "[Our] movement and elections cannot go hand in hand. Participating in elections under [the current government] means to validate them. We cannot continue our movement with those who compete in the elections when the leaders and activists are being arrested and harassed while protesting to free the country from this illegal government. Rather, it is time to identify them and uproot them politically."[[46]](#cite_note-47) On 3 June 2023, the BNP expelled 43 of its leaders for life as a result of their decision to participate in the [Sylhet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet "Sylhet") City Corporation election.[[47]](#cite_note-48)

Jamaat-e-Islami was banned from participating in elections in 2013, and many of its former leaders have gone on to form the [Bangladesh Development Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Development_Party "Bangladesh Development Party") (BDP), which inten

ds to participate in the elections. The president of the BDP, Anwarul Islam Chan, has denied any affiliations with the Jamaat, saying: "The post-[liberation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War "Bangladesh Liberation War") generation was born after independence. We are a political party and not interested in such issues" as opposing Bangladesh's independence from Pakistan.[[48]](#cite_note-49)[[49]](#cite_note-50)

The Awami League, on the other hand, has insisted that a caretaker government would be unconstitutional and that the Election Commission is independent and sanctioned by law.[[27]](#cite_note-aa17Jan2023-28)[[50]](#cite_note-51)

The [Bangladeshi Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Bangladesh) "Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Bangladesh)") asserted "the electoral process will remain under strict vigilance, including by international observers as accredited by the Election Commission."[[51]](#cite_note-52) Bangladesh Foreign Minister [Dr. AK Abdul Momen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK_Abdul_Momen "AK Abdul Momen") said on 10 April 2023, in a meeting with US Secretary of State [Antony Blinken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Blinken "Antony Blinken") that the independent election commission is key to holding fair, transparent elections.[[52]](#cite_note-53)

On 23 May 2023, U.S. Secretary of State [Antony Blinken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Blinken "Antony Blinken") announced a new visa policy vis-a-vis Bangladesh to support the country's goal of holding free, fair, and peaceful national elections. The policy states that the US would "restrict the issuance of visas for any Bangladeshi individual, believed to be responsible for, or complicit in, undermining the democratic election process in Bangladesh", including "current and former Bangladeshi officials, members of pro-government and opposition political parties, and members of law enforcement, the judiciary, and security services". The policy lists actions that would undermine the election process as "vote rigging, voter intimidation, the use of violence to prevent people from exercising their right to freedoms of association and peaceful assembly, and the use of measures designed to prevent political parties, voters, civil society, or the media from disseminating their views".[[53]](#cite_note-54)

The restrictions were meant to act as a signal to the Bangladeshi government to hold democratic elections and to the BNP to participate in the elections, as a boycott of them could lead to instability.[[54]](#cite_note-55) When asked how the US would navigate a situation in which a party that refuses to participate in the national election would later claim that the election was unfair, [US State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_State_Department "US State Department") Principal Deputy Spokesperson Vedant Patel said: "I don't have anything else to get into, as it's an internal, domestic election" and that all the US wants is that it should be free, fair, and reflective of the will of the Bangladeshi people.[[55]](#cite_note-56)

On 1 August 2023, US Ambassador Peter Haas announced after meeting with [Chief Election Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Election_Commissioner_of_Bangladesh "Chief Election Commissioner of Bangladesh") [Kazi Habibul Awal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazi_Habibul_Awal "Kazi Habibul Awal") that a US pre-election monitoring team consisting of experts with previous experience in election monitoring and preparation, would arrive in Bangladesh in October before the election which was subsequently cancelled.[[56]](#cite_note-57)

On 4 August 2023, the United Nations denounced pre-election violence in Bangladesh, calling for police "to refrain from excessive use of force amid recurring violence and mass arrests ahead of general elections". This is a human rights issue concerning violence erupting at opposition rallies in 2023, and the harsh response by police using rubber bullets, tear gas and water cannons. A UN spokesman said: "Police, alongside men in plain clothing, have been seen using hammers, sticks, bats and iron rods, among other objects, to beat protesters". He added that hundreds of people who oppose the government have been arrested before and during the rallies.[[57]](#cite_note-StarAug4-58)

UN concerns have arisen after Sheikh Hasina rejected demands by the BNP and its allies for the government to step down and allow the January election to be held under a neutral caretaker government. The UN has stressed that Hasina's government "must abide by their human rights obligations and allow people to exercise their rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of opinion and expression".[[57]](#cite_note-StarAug4-58)

Responding to the UN statement, [Mahfuz Anam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahfuz_Anam "Mahfuz Anam") commented: "From the looks of it, our two major political parties are preparing for 'glad

Therefore, like dengue, BNP has to be prevented".[[59]](#cite_note-60)

Soon after Mahfuz Anam spoke, there was a meeting in Dhaka of the 14-party alliance led by the Awami League. They announced a rally to be held on 7 August before Awami League HQ on Bangabandhu Avenue. The purpose of the rally is to protest against the "terror and anarchy" of BNP and to "prevent any conspiracy of the BNP-Jamaat". A spokesman said alliance members will take to the streets across the whole country, besides Dhaka.[[60]](#cite_note-61)

On 7 May 2023, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina urged [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") Secretary-General Patricia Scotland to send diversified election observers for the election while stating that her government has made the election commission an independent and powerful institution to strengthen the democratic process in the country.[[61]](#cite_note-62)

A group of human rights organizations wrote to 14 members of [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") urging them to be aware of how the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami have been operating "overtly and covertly in cahoots with terrorist groups, like [Ansar al Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansar_al-Islam_(Bangladesh) "Ansar al-Islam (Bangladesh)"), since 2001".[[62]](#cite_note-63)

Terry Isley, a member of an independent election monitoring [delegation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delegation "Delegation") that visited Bangladesh in August 2023, said that the demand for a caretaker government is unconstitutional and illegal in the present political context of Bangladesh. He also expressed disappointment that the BNP refused to meet with the delegation.[[63]](#cite_note-64)

On 20 September 2023, the [Election Commission of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Election_Commission "Bangladesh Election Commission") received a letter from the European Union stating that it would not send a full-fledged election observation mission to the upcoming general election. The letter said Bangladesh's environment is not suitable for election observation.[[64]](#cite_note-65)[[65]](#cite_note-66) However, in a letter to the Election Commission on 19 October the EU said it would send a 4-member technical team to observe the election.[[66]](#cite_note-67)

On the contrary, Bangladesh’s repeated request to sign a deal about [Teesta River](https://www.ndtv.com/india-news/bangladesh-minister-its-a-shame-teesta-river-deal-stuck-for-11-years-3020864) water sharing has been ignored; the India-Bangladesh border has become the most violent border as Indian Border Security Force (BSF) continue to [kill Bangladeshis](https://www.newagebd.net/article/194758/bangladeshi-shot-dead-by-bsf) in large numbers; [trade gaps](https://thefinancialexpress.com.bd/editorial/reducing-bangladeshs-trade-gap-with-india-1666279118) between the two countries have increased over the years in favor of India; and Bangladesh has not received support from India dealing with the Rohingya refugee crisis. In 2018, responding to a question on whether she wants reciprocation from India, Hasina stated that India will [remember forever](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/India-will-remember-forever-for-what-Bangladesh) what Bangladesh gave it. This unequal relationship has persisted because of India’s unqualified support to the Hasina government. In the wake of the 2014 election, the Foreign Secretary [Sujatha Singh visited Dhaka](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/what-was-sujatha-singhs-message) and allegedly pressured the Jatiya Party, led by General H.M. Ershad, to join the election which was boycotted by all opposition parties. In 2018, although it was evident to the Indian establishment that the Awami League has already “assiduously [subverted](https://www.orfonline.org/research/43844-shadow-of-india-hasina-governments-corruption-repression-of-bnp-looms-over-bangladesh-polls/) democratic norms and institutions” and that in a fair election “the Awami League will be reduced to an embarrassing minority in the next Parliament,” India’s support to the Awami League was unflinching. Such actions contribute to a perception in Bangladesh that India’s support is vital for the survival of the Hasina government. Such suspicion was further cemented when Foreign Minister AK Abdul Momen [said in 2022](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/requested-india-ensure-pm-hasinas-govt-any-cost-momen-479898) that he had asked India to ensure the Hasina government’s survival at any cost.

#### **The follies of Indian media coverage**

Three follies are easily discerned in the arguments of Indian commentators:

1. While they are criticizing the United States for what they are describing as intrusion into Bangladesh’s domestic politics, they conveniently ignore how India has maintained its influence over the past decade and ironically call upon the Indian government to side with the incumbent Hasina regime disregarding their own stated concerns about sovereignty. While the United States has repeatedly reaffirmed that it is not favoring any party over the other but simply underscoring the need for a fair electoral process, the Indian media are asking it to interject on behalf of a specific political party.
2. They are implicitly suggesting that a fair election will deliver a victory to the opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). This concern is difficult to square with their claims that Bangladesh has achieved remarkable economic and social successes in the past fourteen years and that Hasina has the support of most of the population.
3. The argument that a victory of BNP will reignite militancy disregards the global context of the rise of transnational and regional terrorist groups around the world and the changed circumstances. It is not a stretch to suggest that such an argument is nothing short of using Islamist bogeymen to justify undemocratic behavior.

#### **How India assumed the commanding position**

The enormous influence of India over Bangladesh’s domestic politics is a result of a geopolitical game in the region since 2001, and reflects the conspicuous absence of the United States. After the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, the United States remained focused on Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Iraq invasion diverted its attention from South Asia. A growing relationship between the United States and India gave the latter the opportunity to extend its sphere of influence. The United States had seen India as [the antidote to China](https://thewire.in/diplomacy/as-modi-goes-to-washington-india-must-not-lose-sight-of-the-choices-it-faces). As for the Bangladesh policy, despite Washington’s reliance on India, it disagreed with New Delhi on the course of Bangladesh’s democratic trajectory. In 2013-14, New Delhi and Washington went through several rounds of conversations about the need for an inclusive election in Dhaka. Then United States ambassador to Bangladesh, [Dan Mozena](https://bdnews24.com/bangladesh/us-india-talks-on-bangladesh-situation), made several visits to New Delhi, but India took a firmer stand and [rebuffed United States](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/indias-understanding-of-bangladesh-will-help-us/article5516435.ece) efforts. The United States backstepped, allowed India to do its bidding, and the Hasina government continued; however, the United States had not lost sight of the continued regression of human rights and democracy in Bangladesh as reflected in the annual [human rights](https://www.state.gov/reports/2021-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/bangladesh) reports of the State Department.

#### **The United States returns to Bangladesh**

With the Presidency of Joe Biden, democracy and human rights once again are a professedly cornerstone of United States foreign policy. This has spurred a change in [Bangladesh policy](https://www.thedailystar.net/opinion/black-white-and-grey/news/sanctions-against-rab-and-the-shifts-us-policies-2922766). The imposition of [sanctions](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/southasiasource/us-sanctions-on-bangladeshs-rab-what-happened-whats-next/) on Bangladesh’s elite police force, the Rapid Actions Battalion (RAB), and its seven officials in December 2021, and serious [warnings](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/southasiasource/what-the-new-us-visa-policy-for-bangladesh-means/) through 2022 and early 2023, clearly revealed that Bangladesh is being closely watched by the United States administration. The growing [influence of China](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/new-atlanticist/as-the-sino-indian-rivalry-heats-up-watch-bangladesh-carefully/) on Bangladesh since 2016 and United States focus on the Indo-Pacific region enhance the geo-political significance of Bangladesh. As such, the United States seemed to adopt a carrot-and-stick policy towards Bangladesh. The United States donated the largest number of COVID-19 vaccines to Bangladesh, but such largesse was also accompanied by concerns regarding the erosion of democracy. These efforts, which didn’t go through New Delhi, showed that the “US is no longer watching Bangladesh through [the Indian lens](https://news.abplive.com/blog/opinion-us-watching-bangladesh-this-time-not-through-india-lens-pm-sheikh-hasina-1607810?fbclid=IwAR0iqHxj4TyA1VBAFIV026kCy5tVmJ_K1KT5PbyRicxsjhErZpjCnhb4jaY).”

#### **Does the Indian government’s silence bear any message?**

Despite the intense discussions in the media, there hasn’t been any official word from New Delhi regarding the new United States policy or the growing tension between the United States and Bangladesh. New Delhi has remained studiously silent. Unlike in 2014, India is leaving the US-Bangladesh issue out of its public posture. After the imposition of sanctions on RAB, India’s reaction was muted, although Bangladesh sought [India’s help](https://www.dhakatribune.com/nation/2022/04/26/momen-delhis-support-sought-after-us-sanctions-on-rab) to reverse the decision. Many wondered whether New Delhi was consulted on the issue, and there is no indication that New Delhi ever raised the issue with Washington.

Three interpretations of India’s current lack of engagement are worth considering:

1. Despite United States actions demanding a reversal of democratic erosion, New Delhi is comfortable with the status quo. In the past year and a half, as US officials were sending strong messages to Bangladesh regarding the human rights situation and democracy, public messages from India were a show of support to Hasina. Visits of Indian Foreign Secretary [Vinay Khatra](https://en.hirenpandit.com/india-has-full-support-for-sheikh-hasinas-leadership-vinoy-khatra/) in February this year and Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in [April](https://www.kalerkantho.com/english/online/national/2023/05/11/52828) and [May](https://www.news18.com/world/jaishankar-calls-on-bangladesh-pm-sheikh-hasina-in-dhaka-7788397.html), and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s invitation to Hasina as an observer to the [Group of Twenty](https://www.indiatoday.in/india/story/bangladesh-pm-sheikh-hasina-attend-g20-summit-new-delhi-guest-country-2384780-2023-05-26) to be held in New Delhi in September are cases in point.
