Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_Bangladesh:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/State_resources%2C_corruption_and_the_police.jpg/250px-State_resources%2C_corruption_and_the_police.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:State_resources,_corruption_and_the_police.jpg)

A cartoon made by Arifur Rahman in 2008

**Corruption in Bangladesh** has been a continuing problem. Like many other developing and [emerging countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerging_countries "Emerging countries"), corruption is a part of life in Bangladesh. Regular citizens routinely pay bribes for basic services and to skip queues, and officials rely on bribes to make a living.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

As of 2001, corruption in the public sector was "endemic, chronic and all pervasive".[[2]](#cite_note-Zafarullah-2001-2)

The [Anti Corruption Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti_Corruption_Commission_Bangladesh "Anti Corruption Commission Bangladesh") was formed in 2004, but is considered to be largely ineffective in investigating and preventing corruption because of governmental control over it.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4). The Anti Corruption Commission chairman [Iqbal Mahmood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iqbal_Mahmood "Iqbal Mahmood") admitted in November 2020 that "there are high levels of bribery and corruption in government services" in Bangladesh.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International")'s 2025 [Corruption Perceptions Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_Perceptions_Index "Corruption Perceptions Index"), which scored 182 countries on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean"),[[6]](#cite_note-6) Bangladesh scored 24. Bangladesh was ranked among the 13 most corrupt countries globally in the index.[[7]](#cite_note-DailyStar-20260211-7). For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the Index[[Note 1]](#cite_note-9) was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15.[[9]](#cite_note-10) For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie).[[10]](#cite_note-11)

Commenting on Bangladesh's score on the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index in the wake of the August 2024 fall of the authoritarian [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") premiership, Executive Director [Iftekharuzzaman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iftekharuzzaman "Iftekharuzzaman") of [Transparency International Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International_Bangladesh "Transparency International Bangladesh") said in early 2026, "Over the past one and a half years, the interim government has failed to take effective and exemplary action against corruption. At the same time, proposed reforms by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and other institutions have largely been ignored or left unimplemented, weakening their ability to act independently." In south Asia, only Afghanistan ranks lower than Bangladesh, he said.[[7]](#cite_note-DailyStar-20260211-7)

## Causes of corruption

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_in_Bangladesh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Causes of corruption")]

After splitting from Pakistan in 1971, Bangladesh was ruled by a series of civilian and military governments. Riots surrounding the 2014 elections resulted in hundreds of deaths and [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") changed the country's "political rights" rating from 3 to 4 (with 1 being best, 7 worst). This was only one incident, however, in a modern history of highly fatal political violence.[[11]](#cite_note-trans-12)

The country's score for rule of law on the Worldwide Governance Indicators declined from 28.6 (on a scale of 0–100) in 2011 to 22.7 in 2013. Although, Bangladesh has experienced notable social and economic progress since around the turn of the century, it remained one of the world's poorest nations in 2015, with 76.5% of the population living on less than US$2 a day.[[12]](#cite_note-13)

## Corruption by sector

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_in_Bangladesh&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Corruption by sector")]

As of 2001, bribery, misappropriation of funds, excessive lobbying, delays in performing services, pilferage, neglect of duties, abuse of power, and patronage were rampant throughout the public sector. This included law enforcement, customs, tax authorities, banking, education, health care, the judiciary, and utilities.[[2]](#cite_note-Zafarullah-2001-2)[[13]](#cite_note-14)

![](/static/2958550a00127cfea909b6a91493208b/0d82a/CleanedWFB-editions-Screenshot-possible-graphic.jpg)

One of CIA’s oldest and most recognizable intelligence publications, The World Factbook, has sunset. The World Factbook served the Intelligence Community and the general public as a longstanding, one-stop basic reference about countries and communities around the globe. Let’s take a quick look into the history of The World Factbook.

[Over many decades](/stories/story/history-of-the-world-factbook/), The World Factbook evolved from a classified to unclassified, hardcopy to electronic product that added new categories, and even new global entities. The original classified publication, titled *The National Basic Intelligence Factbook*, launched in 1962. The first unclassified companion version was issued in 1971. A decade later it was renamed The World Factbook. In 1997, The World Factbook went digital and debuted to a worldwide audience on CIA.gov, where it garnered millions of views each year.

The World Factbook appealed to researchers, news organizations, teachers, students, and international travelers. Some readers even inquired whether their preferred geographic designation or world entity could be included on the high-profile site.

Finally, only CIA insiders would know that officers donated some of their personal travel photos to The World Factbook, which hosted more than 5,000 photographs that were copyright-free for anyone to access and use.

Though the World Factbook is gone, in the spirit of its global reach and legacy, we hope you will stay curious about the world and find ways to explore it… in person or virtually.

General elections were held in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") on 7 January 2024 in accordance with the [constitutional requirement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bangladesh "Constitution of Bangladesh"), stating that elections must take place within the 90-day period before the expiration of the current term of the [Jatiya Sangsad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatiya_Sangsad "Jatiya Sangsad") on 29 January 2024. The [Awami League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League"), led by incumbent [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina"), won the election for the fourth consecutive time with less than 40% of the eligible voters voting according to an Election Commission, which was run by the ruling political party.[[4]](#cite_note-:3-5)[[5]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[6]](#cite_note-7)[[7]](#cite_note-:BBC-8) The party won 224 seats while independent candidates, most of whom were Awami League members propped up as [dummy candidates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_candidate "Dummy candidate") to give a semblance of competition, won 62 seats.[[8]](#cite_note-9)[[9]](#cite_note-:4-10)[[10]](#cite_note-11)

In the lead-up to the election, the incumbent government led by [Sheikh Hasina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Hasina "Sheikh Hasina") cracked down on opposition parties and silenced critics of the government.[[11]](#cite_note-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13)[[13]](#cite_note-:2-14) Hasina's prime ministership has been described as authoritarian since being re-elected in 2008,[[14]](#cite_note-15)[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17)[[17]](#cite_note-18) and in 2011 removed the requirement that a temporary independent [caretaker government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caretaker_government "Caretaker government") be formed to hold elections. The main opposition party, the [Bangladesh Nationalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Nationalist_Party "Bangladesh Nationalist Party"), boycotted the elections (as they did in 2014) as they assumed that the election commission under the incumbent government were unable to organise a free and fair election.[[13]](#cite_note-:2-14)

A protest over the election turnout emerged as the Chief Election Commissioner initially claimed, based on the data at hand, that turnout was 28%, but later retracted that statement to claim turnout was around 40%.[[9]](#cite_note-:4-10)[[7]](#cite_note-:BBC-8)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Bangladesh:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Flag_of_Bangladesh.jpg/330px-Flag_of_Bangladesh.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_Bangladesh.jpg)

[Flag of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Bangladesh "Flag of Bangladesh")

**Human rights in Bangladesh** are enshrined as [fundamental rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_rights_in_Bangladesh "Fundamental rights in Bangladesh") in Part III of the [Constitution of Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bangladesh "Constitution of Bangladesh"). However, constitutional and legal experts believe many of the country's laws require reform to enforce [fundamental rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_rights_of_the_people_of_Bangladesh "Fundamental rights of the people of Bangladesh") and reflect [democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy") values of the 21st century.

During the period from 2009 to 2023 under the rule of the [Awami League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League")-led regime, 2,699 people were victims of [extrajudicial killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killing "Extrajudicial killing") in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](#cite_note-:23-1) During the same time frame, 677 people were [forcibly disappeared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance"), and 1,048 people died in custody.[[1]](#cite_note-:23-1) These statistics were revealed by the [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") organization [Odhikar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odhikar "Odhikar"). Additionally, the organization claims that if the deaths from the [anti-discrimination student protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Bangladesh_quota_reform_movement "2024 Bangladesh quota reform movement") and incidents from 2024 are included, the total death toll would exceed 3,000.[[1]](#cite_note-:23-1)

In 2024, [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") rated Bangladesh's human rights at 40 out 100 (partly free).[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Reforms were proposed in 2017 and included strengthening [parliamentary supremacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_supremacy "Parliamentary supremacy"), [judicial independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence"), the [separation of powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers "Separation of powers"), repealing laws which restrain [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press") and disbanding security agencies which violate civil liberties.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Even though Bangladesh has [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") as its [state religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion") and has constitutional references to [Hindus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindus "Hindus"), [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") and [Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhists "Buddhists"); the political system is modeled as a [secular democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular_democracy "Secular democracy"). Governments have generally respected [freedom of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion"),[[7]](#cite_note-7) a cornerstone of the Bangladeshi constitution. However, the police have been slow in responding to and investigating attacks against minorities, opposition activists & supporters and purportedly suppress protests against the government. According to Human Right Watch, around five hundred people have been disappeared since last ten years. In southeastern Bangladesh, the [Chittagong Hill Tracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Hill_Tracts "Chittagong Hill Tracts") remains a militarized region due to a historical insurgency. Tribal people in Bangladesh have demanded constitutional recognition.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

According to Dr. Mizanur Rahman, the former chairman of the National Human Rights Commission, 70% of allegations of human rights violations are against law enforcement agencies (2015).[[9]](#cite_note-9) [Torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture") and [enforced disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearances_in_Bangladesh "Enforced disappearances in Bangladesh") are rampantly employed by Bangladeshi security forces. In recent years,[*[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] [free speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_speech "Free speech") and media freedom have been repressed by the government through laws regulating newspapers, TV channels and the internet. Elected MPs in parliament lack voting freedoms. The future of [elect

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearances_in_Bangladesh:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Forced_disappearance-bangladesh-1.jpg/250px-Forced_disappearance-bangladesh-1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Forced_disappearance-bangladesh-1.jpg)

Mother of Sajedul Islam Sumon holding his picture in 2013



**Extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances in Bangladesh** refer to [extrajudicial executions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossfire_(Bangladesh) "Crossfire (Bangladesh)") carried out by law enforcement agencies without due legal process and to [abduction cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance") in which the [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Bangladesh "Government of Bangladesh") directly or indirectly kidnaps people and holds them incommunicado.[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) From 2009 to 2023, at least 2,699 people were victims of [extrajudicial killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killing "Extrajudicial killing") in the 160-million-strong Bangladesh.[[3]](#cite_note-:22-3) During the period, 677 people were forcibly disappeared, and 1,048 people died in custody.[[3]](#cite_note-:22-3) From 2004 to 2006, at least 991 people were killed extrajudicially by "death squad" the [Rapid Action Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_Action_Battalion "Rapid Action Battalion") (RAB).[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) The practice of extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances primarily involves law enforcement agencies such as the RAB and the [Detective Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detective_Branch "Detective Branch") (DB) of the police.

These practices began during the administration of [Sheikh Mujibur Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Mujibur_Rahman "Sheikh Mujibur Rahman") and continued through subsequent regimes, including those of General Ershad and the government of the [Bangladesh Nationalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Nationalist_Party "Bangladesh Nationalist Party").[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) During its tenure from 2009 to 2024, the [Awami League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League") government has been particularly noted for using such tactics to control dissent, even during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and human rights groups, including [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") and [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International"), repeatedly appeal to the government to stop these human rights violations, but to no avail.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) In 2021, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") imposed sanctions on the RAB and its seven high officials.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Since the imposition of the US sanctions, the number of extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances has begun decreasing.

In 2016, the families of the victims of enforced disappearance in Bangladesh founded a platform *[Mayer Daak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayer_Daak "Mayer Daak")* to press their demand to know the whereabouts of their loved ones who disappeared under mysterious situation.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) On 14 August 2022, [Netra News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netra_News "Netra News"), which was then blocked in Bangladesh, published a whistleblower report alleging that Bangladesh officials were holding and torturing victims of enforced disappearances at [Aynaghar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aynaghar "Aynaghar"), a secret detention facility.

After the downfall of the Awami league government in a [mass uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%E2%80%93People's_uprising "Student–People's uprising") on 5 August 2024, the interim government led by [Muhammad Yunus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Yunus "Muhammad Yunus") formed a five-member inquiry commission on 27 August 2024, to investigate extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances.[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11) Headed by a retired high court judge, the commission was tasked with investigating the activities of the police, the RAB, the [Border Guard Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Guard_Bangladesh "Border Guard Bangladesh") (BGB), the [Criminal Investigation Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Investigation_Department_(Bangladesh) "Criminal Investigation Department (Bangladesh)") (CID), the [Special Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Branch_(Bangladesh) "Special Branch (Bangladesh)") (SB), the [National Security Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Intelligence "National Security Intelligence") (NSI) and the military's [Directorate General of Forces Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate_General_of_Forces_Intelligence "Directorate General of

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Mayer Daak** ([Bengali](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): মায়ের ডাক, [lit.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'Mother’s Call') is a platform of the families of the people who fell victim to [enforced disappearance](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killings_and_enforced_disappearances_in_Bangladesh "Extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances in Bangladesh") allegedly by government agencies during the rule of the [Awami League](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awami_League "Awami League") led government from 2009 to until date in [Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](#cite_note-1) The platform was launched with the common interest of the family members of the victims of enforced disappearance in Bangladesh to learn the fate of their beloved one, who went missing after men in plainclothes posing as law enforcers picked them up from various places of the country.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The platform, largely consists of the family members of [Bangladesh Nationalist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Nationalist_Party "Bangladesh Nationalist Party") leaders since most of the victims had political affiliation with the party, observes the "International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances" every year in Bangladesh.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

According to local rights groups, more than 500 people disappeared after being picked up by government agencies since 2009 in Bangladesh.[[4]](#cite_note-4) [Human Rights Watch](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") published a report on the victims of enforced disappearance in Bangladesh that stated that they have recorded at least 90 cases of enforced disappearance only in 2016.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Mayer Daak is similar to that of [Argentina](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina")'s [Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothers_of_the_Plaza_de_Mayo "Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo") which was founded by [Argentine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentine "Argentine") mothers whose children "disappeared" during the state terrorism of the military dictatorship, between 1976 and 1983.

[Bangladesh Awami League](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Awami_League "Bangladesh Awami League") came to power after winning the national election of December 2008 against the backdrop of a turmoil political condition after two consecutive regimes of BNP (2001–2006) and military-backed civil government (2007–2008) who were largely criticized for promoting [extrajudicial killing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killing "Extrajudicial killing") with a view to reducing crime.

Prior to the election, Awami League promised to put an end to the spate of extrajudicial killing by government agencies and custodial deaths. However, this practice never ended.

In 2010, due to the former Prime Minister and BNP chief [Begum Khaleda Zia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begum_Khaleda_Zia "Begum Khaleda Zia")’s eviction from her house, BNP started taking streets while on the other hand, their ally Jamaat-e-Islami supporters started demanding the release of their leaders who were involved in war-crime during [Liberation War of Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_War_of_Bangladesh "Liberation War of Bangladesh").

For its first three decades, the IMF oversaw the [Bretton Woods system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system "Bretton Woods system") of [fixed exchange rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_exchange_rate "Fixed exchange rate") arrangements. World map of countries or territories by [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") scores in increments of 0.050 (based on 2023 data, published in 2025):

* ≥ 0.950

The [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") (HDI) is the most widely used indicator of human development and has changed how people view the concept.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-quartz-2) However, several aspects of the index have received criticism. Some scholars have criticized how the factors are weighed, in particular how an additional year of [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") is valued differently between countries;[[2]](#cite_note-quartz-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) and the limited factors it considers, noting the omission of factors such as the levels of distributional and [gender inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_inequality "Gender inequality").[[4]](#cite_note-4) In response to the former, the UNDP introduced the [inequality-adjusted Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_inequality-adjusted_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by inequality-adjusted Human Development Index") (IHDI) in its 2010 report, and in response to the latter the [Gender Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_Development_Index "Gender Development Index") (GDI) was introduced in the 1995 report.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Others have criticized the perceived oversimplification of using a single number per country.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-SHDI-8)

To reflect developmental differences within countries, a subnational HDI (SHDI) featuring data for more than 1,600 regions was introduced in 2018 by the Global Data Lab at [Radboud University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radboud_University_Nijmegen "Radboud University Nijmegen") in the Netherlands.[[8]](#cite_note-SHDI-8) In 2020, the UNDP introduced another index, the [planetary pressures–adjusted Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_planetary_pressures%E2%80%93adjusted_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by planetary pressures–adjusted Human Development Index") (PHDI), which decreases the scores of countries with a higher ecological footprint.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Dimensions and indicators

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Dimensions and indicators")]

The HDI was first published in 1990 with the goal of being a more comprehensive measure of human development than purely economic measures such as [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product"). The index incorporates three dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and decent living standards. Various [indicators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indicator_(statistics) "Indicator (statistics)") are used to quantify how countries perform on each dimension. The indicators used in the 2022 report were [life expectancy at birth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy"); expected years of schooling for children; mean years of schooling for adults; and [gross national income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_national_income "Gross national income") per capita. The indicators are used to create a health index, an education index and an income index, each with a value between 0 and 1. The [geometric mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_mean "Geometric mean") of the three indices—that is, the cube root of the product of the indices—is the human development index. A value above 0.800 is classified as very high, between 0.700 and 0.799 as high, 0.550 to 0.699 as medium, and below 0.550 as low.[[10]](#cite_note-overview-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note

The **Rapid Action Battalion** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): র‍্যাপিড অ্যাকশন ব্যাটালিয়ন, [romanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Bengali "Romanization of Bengali"): *Ryaepid Ækśon Byāṭāliẏan*; abbreviated as **RAB**) is an elite [law enforcement force in Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_Bangladesh "Law enforcement in Bangladesh") tasked with combating serious crimes, terrorism, and organised criminal activities. Operating under the [Ministry of Home Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Home_Affairs_(Bangladesh) "Ministry of Home Affairs (Bangladesh)"), RAB is a composite force comprising personnel from the [Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Police "Bangladesh Police"), [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Army "Bangladesh Army"), [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Navy "Bangladesh Navy"), [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Air_Force "Bangladesh Air Force"), [BGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Guard_Bangladesh "Border Guard Bangladesh"), and [Ansar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Ansar "Bangladesh Ansar"). Since its establishment in 2004, RAB has played a key role in counter-terrorism, anti-drug operations, and high-profile criminal investigations.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

The Rapid Action Battalion has faced criticism from [human rights groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_group "Human rights group") for their alleged involvement in [extrajudicial killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killing "Extrajudicial killing") and [enforced disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance").[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) It is estimated that between 2004 and 2008, RAB had killed 1,062 people.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
